name: Colin Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and nothing goes out with your name on it. I'll describe five pictures of the future and ask what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the Greenfield Co-op on Station Road, which is a member-owned supermarket, so the shoppers who pay the yearly fee technically own it. I do tills from noon, then from six I'm stacking shelves in dairy and frozen until close. I'm still learning, to be honest. Last week I put the oat milk where the soya should go and a woman spent ten minutes telling me about her allergies.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the Co-op pays a bit above the other supermarkets and there's a members' meeting where staff can vote too. What wears me out is the freezer aisle at nine at night, my hands go numb. My partner Aisha is a nurse, and we lived cheap for years, so we've got about a year of costs put away. That's mostly because I stayed in my parents' back room till I was 25.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fair enough, it was hype, and I'm glad. At work I'd joke that the new AI stock-counting app still can't find the oat milk either. Online I'd probably share something about the money spent on hype going to wages instead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's basically nothing. I use AI sometimes to write a letter to the landlord or plan meals, and that'd carry on. My real question would still be whether I want to stack shelves at forty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my hours and probably sign up for the electrician pre-apprenticeship course at the college that I keep looking at. It's two evenings a week for a year, and I'd pay for it out of savings. Aisha and I would keep saving for a deposit on a flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Kind of nice, actually. It takes one worry off the pile and leaves the normal ones.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You keep looking at that course but haven't signed up. What's stopped you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Seeing if it's worth it, really. My mate Rob did it and now he's on a proper apprenticeship, so I've seen it work for someone. That's how I do things, I wait till I've seen someone do it first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: In this world, would you still bother with the Co-op members' meetings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, because they decide things like whether we get more staff on Saturdays. Nobody young goes, so the old members vote for whatever the manager suggests. I'd go just to be a different face.

say: I'd say it was **hype**, and the stock app still can't find the **oat milk**.
I'd post that hype money should go to **wages** instead.
think: For me almost **nothing changes**, beyond letters and meal plans with AI.
My real question is whether I want to **stack shelves at forty**.
do: Sign up for the **electrician pre-apprenticeship**, two evenings a week for a year.
Pay the course fee from **savings** and keep my Co-op hours.
Keep saving with Aisha toward a **flat deposit**.
feel: **Calm**, with one worry taken off the pile.
S0.quote: My real question would still be whether I want to stack shelves at forty.
fieldNote: His career doubt exists **without AI**, which shapes every answer.
He moves once a **friend has proven** the path, like Rob did.
He sees the **members' meeting** as a real lever for staff.

steps.text: Enrol in the college electrician pre-apprenticeship evening course
Attend the Co-op members' meeting and vote on staffing

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the Co-op should be the one shop that does this fairly, because the members own it. At the members' meeting I'd ask what happens to staff when the ordering and the phone line go to software. Online I'd share stuff about unions getting a say on new tech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My tills and shelves don't change much at first, robots are slow in this one. But the Co-op office would shrink, and those people would want shop floor hours. So the job isn't gone, it just gets more crowded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd definitely do the electrician course now, no more waiting. I'd join the shop workers' union properly, because right now I only pay into the Co-op staff group. I'd learn the new ordering app they'd bring in, so I'm the one who can fix it when it plays up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not panicking, just the feeling of the floor tilting a little.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If the Co-op asked staff to vote on cutting office jobs for software, how would you vote?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd vote no unless they had a plan for every person, like moving them to the shop floor or paying for training. That's the point of a co-op. If the Co-op acts like every other chain, why have members?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone at work you'd worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pauline in the office, who does all the ordering by phone and knows every supplier by first name. Ordering is exactly what the software would take first. Pauline is 55 and I don't think she'd find another office job easily.

say: I'd say a **member-owned** shop should handle this **fairly**.
I'd ask the members' meeting what happens to **office staff** when software takes ordering.
think: My tills change slowly, but office people would want **shop floor hours**.
The job isn't gone, it just gets more **crowded**.
do: Start the **electrician course** now instead of waiting.
Join the **shop workers' union** properly, not just the staff group.
Learn the new **ordering app** so I'm useful when it breaks.
feel: **Uneasy**, like the floor tilting a little.
S1.quote: If the Co-op acts like every other chain, why have members?
fieldNote: He sees the co-op model as a **test** of fair change.
His worry goes first to **Pauline**, an older colleague in ordering.
He mixes **collective action** with a personal hedge in the trades.

steps.text: Start the electrician pre-apprenticeship course this autumn
Join the shop workers' union instead of only the staff group
Learn the new Co-op ordering app inside out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need to move now, not in 2030, and I'd be at every protest about it. I'd tell everyone that robots on the shop floor by 2031 means millions of shop jobs, not a few. Online I'd be the annoying one sharing petitions every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think my till job is done by about 2031. AGI in 2028 does the office side, and then three years later the robots do mine. Being an electrician might buy me a few more years, because someone has to wire the robots in, but even that's not forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first year I'd go full time on an electrician apprenticeship, even though the pay drops, and use our savings to cover the gap. I'd keep one weekend shift at the Co-op for the money. Aisha and I would put the flat on hold, because I don't want a mortgage on a wage that could vanish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I've got money and a plan, so it's not panic, but the plan has a short shelf life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Aisha is a nurse. Does her job feel safer to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For a while, yes. Robots lifting patients and changing dressings as well as a nurse feels far off, even in 2031. So we'd lean on her wage and I'd be the one taking the risk on retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my dad not to worry, because he always worries. Then I'd ask if I could keep my stuff in their garage if we had to downsize. That back room has saved me before.

say: I'd say governments must act **now**, not in 2030.
I'd warn that **shop floor robots** by 2031 hit millions of jobs, not a few.
think: My **till job** is likely done by about 2031.
Electrical work buys **a few more years**, wiring robots in, but not forever.
do: Move to a **full-time apprenticeship** and cover the pay gap from savings.
Keep one **weekend shift** at the Co-op.
feel: **Anxious**, with money and a plan but a short **shelf life**.
S2.quote: Being an electrician might buy me a few more years, because someone has to wire the robots in, but even that's not forever.
fieldNote: He uses the **3-year gap** to jump to a trade before robots arrive.
He leans on **Aisha's nursing wage** as the steady income.
Housing plans are **frozen** to avoid debt on uncertain pay.

steps.text: Start a full-time electrician apprenticeship, covering the gap from savings
Keep one weekend shift at the Co-op
Pause the flat deposit plan with Aisha
Join protests calling for a government transition plan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to start, but only if we start right now. At the Co-op I'd ask the members to set up a retraining fund for staff. Online I'd keep pushing for rules on how fast shops can bring robots in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can finish an apprenticeship before 2034, which is a real difference. Four years of training, then a few years of work before robots catch up with electricians too. It's not safe, but it's a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship next year, part time at first, so I keep some Co-op hours. I'd put a fixed amount aside every month for the gap years. I'd use AI tools more for studying the theory, because I'm slow at the maths.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but working on it. Five years is enough to be busy, which helps more than it should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a retraining fund. Would the members actually vote for that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, if it came out of the profit share we get at Christmas. Most members are retired and they like the staff. I'd have to make the case like it's about their shop, not about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And what changes once the robots arrive around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By then I'd hope to be qualified and doing installs or maintenance. If the robots are good enough to rewire a house, then we're all in the same boat. At that point it's about what the government does, not me.

say: I'd say five years works only if we **start now**.
I'd ask Co-op members to fund **staff retraining**.
think: I can finish an **apprenticeship before 2034**, which makes a real difference.
It's not safe, but it's a **bridge** to a few more working years.
do: Start a **part-time apprenticeship** next year and keep some Co-op hours.
Set aside a **fixed amount monthly** for the training years.
Use AI tools to study the **maths** I'm slow at.
feel: **Anxious**, but busy enough that it helps.
S3.quote: If the robots are good enough to rewire a house, then we're all in the same boat.
fieldNote: Five years lets him **finish training** before robots arrive.
He'd frame a retraining fund around the **members' own shop**.
Beyond 2034 he hands the problem to **government**.

steps.text: Begin a part-time electrician apprenticeship next year
Set a fixed monthly transfer into a training fund
Propose a staff retraining fund at the Co-op members' meeting
Use an AI tutor for apprenticeship maths

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, so don't waste it. I'd want unions and the Co-op to plan properly, with training budgets and dates. I'd be less shouty online and more practical.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can do the whole thing calmly: apprenticeship, qualify, work a few years, maybe even start my own small electrical business. By 2039 I'd be 40. Whatever happens then, I'd have savings and a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the apprenticeship within two years, after saving a bit more. Aisha and I would probably go ahead with the flat, just a cheaper one. I'd keep using AI tools for paperwork and quotes once I'm qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly calm, with a little question mark. Ten years is long enough to make a life in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you wait to see others do something first. Would ten years make you wait too long?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably a bit, yeah. Aisha would kick me if I waited more than two. Rob from college would too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about colleagues like Pauline in the office?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years Pauline could retire nearly on time, which is the best case. I'd still push the Co-op to give her training if her ordering job goes first. Ten years only helps the people who use it.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, so don't waste it.
I'd push for **training budgets** with real dates, less shouting.
think: I can **qualify calmly** and maybe start a small **electrical business**.
By 2039 I'd be **40**, with savings and a trade.
do: Start the **apprenticeship** within two years after saving more.
Use AI for **quotes and paperwork** once qualified.
S4.quote: Ten years only helps the people who use it.
fieldNote: Even calm, he admits his habit of **waiting too long**.
Aisha and his friend Rob act as his **push to move**.
He still worries about **Pauline** losing her ordering job first.

steps.text: Save for a year, then start an electrician apprenticeship
Buy a cheaper flat with Aisha
Push the Co-op for a dated staff training budget

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because it doesn't give me time to finish a trade before robots hit the shop floor. What would help is paid apprenticeships for adults, so I'm not living off savings at 28. And a real plan from the government instead of press releases.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about partners. Half of what I'd do depends on my partner Aisha's nursing job staying steady. If nursing went too, I'd be answering every question differently.

headlineQuote: Half of what I'd do depends on my partner Aisha's nursing job staying steady.
portrait: Colin is a **27-year-old** till and shelf worker at a member-owned co-op supermarket.
He and his partner Aisha, a nurse, have **a year saved**, mostly from years in his parents' house.
He changes once **others have proven** a path, and his electrician course is that path.
He's calm in **AI Plateau**, uneasy in Steady Disruption and **anxious** in the fast AGI pictures.
He mixes **co-op votes** and union action with a personal move into the trades.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, which leaves no time to finish a trade before robots reach shops.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid adult apprenticeships** so retraining doesn't drain savings.
A real **government plan** instead of press releases.
